attempts.label: DANDI:000054
attempts.paper_title: Experience-dependent contextual codes in the hippocampus
attempts.entry_title: Experience-dependent contextual codes in the hippocampus (Plitt and Giocomo 2021)
attempts.summary: In this data the paper's inference findings largely held up: population similarity on S-tilde 0.25 trials differs between rare and frequent morph mice, the codes stay distinct along the track, session estimates lean toward their own condition's posterior, and a Hebbian network trained on each prior reproduces this. Frequent morph values were smaller than the paper's, and priors reconstructed from neural data missed the rare prior, which the Methods formula cannot recover on this design. Abrupt against gradual remapping did not reproduce as measured: the place-cell similarity test fails under the claims file's smoothing, and a block measure the paper does not define does not separate the groups. The files also yield about 60% more place cells than reported.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Plitt and Giocomo (2021) on dandiset 000054, which holds the two-photon imaging of CA1 and the aligned virtual reality behaviour of 16 mice running morphed linear tracks. Part 1 covers sessions, licking, place cells, their similarity matrices, NMF and UMAP; part 2 covers the link to the authors' VR deposit on figshare and the training trials, population similarity, the similarity fraction, Q estimates, prior reconstruction, the decision mice and the two models.

outcomes.statement: Each imaging session recorded between 161 and 3,657 putative CA1 pyramidal cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 1; Methods, Two-photon imaging; Extended Data Fig. 1a,b
outcomes.quote: In each session, we were able to simultaneously image up to several thousands (range of 161–3,657) of putative CA1 pyramidal cells
outcomes.notes: Over the sessions the paper describes as imaged (1, 3 and 8 to N), rare and frequent morph mice have 161 (F3 session 8) to 3,653 (F6 session 3) cells per session, and adding the decision mice changes neither bound; both are within tolerance under readings (a) and (b). The dandiset also holds imaging of sessions 5 and 7, which the paper does not describe; with them the maximum is 4,103 (F6 session 5), outside the tolerance.
deviations: The files of sessions 5 and 7 (and R4 session 6) are left out of the main count because the paper lists imaging on sessions 1, 3 and 8 to N only; the count over every file is shown.

outcomes.statement: The analyses of sessions 8 to N use 24 rare morph and 21 frequent morph sessions, holding 2,610 and 1,986 trials; the four decision mice contribute 2,460 trials.
outcomes.source: Figure 3c,d legend; Figure 6b,c legend; Extended Data Fig. 10g legend
outcomes.inferred: Counts read from three legends (Fig. 3c,d "n = 24 sessions", "n = 21 sessions"; Fig. 6b "n = 2,610 trials"; Fig. 6c "n = 1,986 trials"; Extended Data Fig. 10g "N = 2,460 trials"); no sentence states them together. Fig. 4e gives 19 frequent sessions, in conflict with 21.
outcomes.notes: Four of the five counts are within tolerance (rare 26 sessions and 2,800 trials, frequent 21 sessions and 1,986 trials). The decision mice contribute 3,217 trials over every imaged session (reading a) and 2,022 over sessions 8 to N (reading b), both outside 2,460 +- 246, so no reading has every count within tolerance; the criterion names no partial outcome, so the outcome is not reproduced (it was partially reproduced before the first verification round). FD3 has no session after 7 in the dandiset. The 2020 code selects the decision mice's imaging sessions from the third on (SFReg, first_ind=2, which printed trial N 2460); here that is sessions 5 and later, 29 sessions and 2,662 trials, within tolerance. It is a variant, not a reading the criterion names, and a question asks a reader whether it should be one. The per-session decision-mouse trial table is printed.
deviations: The dandiset holds two more rare morph sessions 8 to N than the paper counts (26 against 24); all are used.

outcomes.statement: The sessions of the authors' VR deposit on figshare can be matched to the dandiset's imaging sessions of the rare and frequent morph mice, by mouse alias and trial sequence.
outcomes.source: Header M7 (answer of 2026-10-22); figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31974756.v1 (morph_vr_data.zip, behavior.sqlite and one VR sqlite file per session); code src/morph_analyses/mouse_metadata.py at 9230b0a (aliases of R1 to F6)
outcomes.notes: A link claim added in this revision, as the answer of 2026-10-22 makes the authors' figshare VR deposit the source of the priors (M7) and of training-intermediate-fraction. All 89 NWB files of the 12 rare and frequent morph mice match exactly one deposit file of their own mouse (alias of the 2026 code) and no file of another mouse; in each the deposit file holds exactly the NWB trials (offset 0, same count), with S-tilde and the three jitters identical (largest difference 0.0), and every matched file carries the database's imaging flag. No NWB file names an alias, so the alias mapping comes from the 2026 code and the trial sequences confirm it. The deposit holds 352 files of the 12 mice on the task track (one listed twice in its database, none missing from the zip), and 26 files with the imaging flag that match no NWB file (12 of them R6's). Session numbers (added after the first verification round). The file day equals the ordinal of the matched file's date among the mouse's task-track dates in the deposit for 60 of 89 files; for R1 to R4, R6 and F4 the imaging sessions 8 to N fall one date later (two for R6), as the deposit holds eight task-track dates before session 8 for these mice (nine for R6), one more than sessions 1 to 7. The 2020 code's session selection rebuilt from the deposit's imaging flags holds every NWB session 8 to N and more (33 rare, 24 frequent; 2,880 and 2,181 NWB trials against the code's printed 2,540 and 1,986), so it does not identify the two extra rare sessions.

outcomes.statement: Before session 8, rare morph mice had fewer than 4% of trials with intermediate morph values, while frequent morph mice had 60%.
outcomes.source: Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 4; Figure 1d,e
outcomes.quote: mice experienced very few trials with intermediate morph values (shared S ~ = 0.25 − 0.75 ) during the first 7 training sessions (<4% of trials with intermediate morph values before session 8 ... mice were frequently exposed to trials with intermediate morph values (60% of trials with intermediate morph values before session 8
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. The claim was blocked (data_missing), as the dandiset holds only the imaged trials; the answer makes it `data elsewhere`, counted from the figshare deposit, which holds every session. Trials before session 8 are every trial of the mouse's sessions on the task track dated before session 8 (date from vr-deposit-link), and of the earlier session numbers of that date; 15 to 22 sessions over 8 to 10 days per mouse. Reading (a), pooled, holds, rare 3.49% (340 of 9,753 trials) below 4% and frequent 59.83% (5,700 of 9,527) within 0.06 of 60%. Reading (b) does not, as R4 (4.12%) and R6 (5.66%) are above 4%; the other rare mice are 1.85% to 3.15% and the frequent mice 59.2% to 60.6%. The 2026 code's variants (sessions with more than 40 rewards; sessions within 8 days of the first) give 3.41% and 3.19% rare and 59.8% frequent pooled. The dandiset's imaged trials, the earlier run's reference, give 13.85% rare.
deviations: Sessions with few rewards are kept, as the criterion counts every trial; the code's filter of more than 40 rewards is shown as a variant.
outcomes.where: figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31974756.v1 (Unprocessed VR data, the authors' deposit of all VR behaviour)

outcomes.statement: Place cells tiled the track in both conditions; 15,829 rare morph place cells (43% of recorded cells; 23% S-tilde = 0 and 21% S-tilde = 1 place cells) and 8,933 frequent morph place cells (30%; 11% and 10%).
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: rare = 15,829 place cells across all S ~ values, 43% of recorded population, 23% of cells S ~ = 0 place cells, 21% of cells S ~ = 1 place cells; frequent = 8,933 place cells across all S ~ values, 30% of recorded population, 11% of cells S ~ = 0 place cells, 10% of cells S ~ = 1 place cells
outcomes.notes: The recorded cells match the paper's implied totals (36,550 rare and 30,018 frequent against about 36,800 and 29,800), but more of them are place cells under every reading. With low-speed frames left out (reading a, pooled) rare 25,053 (68.5%; 39.2% for S-tilde 0 and 36.0% for S-tilde 1) and frequent 17,025 (56.7%; 24.0% and 24.1%); with all frames (reading b) rare 21,945 (60.0%; 31.0%, 28.2%) and frequent 14,345 (47.8%; 17.8%, 16.3%). Per-session means give the same. None of the eight values is within tolerance under any combination. The place cells of the authors' 2026 code stored in the files give rare 61.5% and frequent 48.6% and agree with reading (b) for about 96% of cell and S-tilde pairs. Tiling of the track is not tested by the criterion. After the first verification round two checks were added. With the 2020 code's signal for place cells, each cell divided by its 95th percentile, the fractions agree within 0.001 (rare 68.5% and frequent 56.7% with low-speed frames left out, 60.0% and 47.7% with all frames) and 99.91% of cell and S-tilde decisions are unchanged, so the signal does not explain the excess; no cell has a 95th percentile of 0. The numba shuffle gives the same exceedance counts as a plain numpy version in 500 of 500 entries (first 50 cells of F3 session 8, 1,000 shuffles, no early stopping). Header M2 says a per-cell scale does not change spatial information, which does not hold in general for the code's +0.001; a question asks a reader about it.
deviations: Spatial information follows the code as the criterion says, including its normalisation by the mean over bins; in the shuffles the minimum subtracted is the real map's minimum over all cells, which is 0 in every session and S-tilde.
A cell stops its shuffles once more than 50 of them reach its SI for every S-tilde and both readings; the decision is the same as after 1,000 shuffles.

outcomes.statement: A smaller proportion of recorded cells were place cells in the frequent morph than in the rare morph condition.
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 4a
outcomes.quote: The proportion of recorded cells that were classified as place cells was smaller in the frequent morph compared to the rare morph condition
outcomes.notes: Under every reading the frequent morph fraction is below the rare morph fraction for any S-tilde and for S-tilde 0 and 1 (pooled, reading a, 0.567 against 0.685, 0.240 against 0.392, 0.241 against 0.360). Per mouse the ranges overlap (reading a, rare 0.62 to 0.79, frequent 0.41 to 0.71).

outcomes.statement: The fraction of cells that are place cells in both S-tilde = 0 and S-tilde = 1 trials (6.07% rare, 1.98% frequent) slightly exceeds the overlap expected of independent populations (4.78% and 1.06%), so the two extreme maps are largely independent (global remapping).
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4a
outcomes.quote: Specifically, 6.07% and 1.98% of recorded cells had significant spatial information in both environments for rare morph and frequent morph sessions, respectively (chance 4.78% and 1.06%, respectively; one-sample two-sided t -test of actual minus chance overlap, t =−4.87, P = 1.37×10 −5 , N = 45 sessions pooled across all mice)

statistics.test: one-sample two-sided t-test of actual minus chance overlap

outcomes.notes: The test holds, t = -10.08, p = 3.2e-13 (reading a) and t = -7.67, p = 9.2e-10 (reading b) over 47 sessions, with actual overlap above chance in 44 of 47. The four values are outside tolerance under every reading, as the place-cell fractions are higher than the paper's; the values given are reading (b), pooled. The median session's overlap is 1.15 to 1.19 times chance, so the maps are largely independent, as stated.
deviations: 47 sessions, where the paper's test used 45.

outcomes.statement: Cells with place fields in both extreme environments (2,219 rare, 594 frequent) tended to cluster at the end points of the track and in the reward zone.
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 4b,c
outcomes.quote: Cells with place fields in both extreme environments tended to cluster at the end points of the track and the reward zone
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. The criterion now names the peak readings (i) each environment's peaks against their own reference and (ii) cells with both peaks in the regions against the product of the references, with reference (b) per environment; the earlier run compared both peaks with the S-tilde 0 place cells. Under the new readings 44 of the 48 combinations (two speed readings, two end-point readings, three peak readings, two references, two conditions) hold. Against the track share every combination holds (ratios 1.41 to 1.87 for separate peaks, 2.12 to 3.48 for both peaks). The four that fail are all reading (i) against reference (b) with the end points as the first and last bin, rare S-tilde 0 peaks 0.577 against 0.585 (low-speed frames left out) and 0.618 against 0.627 (all frames), and frequent S-tilde 0 and 1 peaks 0.619 against 0.635 and 0.574 against 0.601 (low-speed frames left out). Where the overlap cells exceed the place cells of their environment it is by at most 10% (ratios 1.004 to 1.098), so all place cells cluster there. The counts (reading a 5,997 and 2,552; reading b 3,759 and 1,272) are above the paper's 2,219 and 594 and outside tolerance; the measured values are reading (a). Reference (b) counts the overlap cells among the place cells of their environment, which pulls the share and the reference together; the criterion's wording allows it, and the four failing ratios lie between 0.955 and 0.986.
deviations: Both speed readings of M3 are required to hold, as for every place-cell claim.

outcomes.statement: Rare morph place cells keep their map up to a threshold morph value (S about 0.25 to 0.5) and then switch coherently, while frequent morph place cells change gradually; the difference shows in the place-cell similarity matrices across S-tilde values.
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 3; Figure 2e-h
outcomes.quote: In the rare morph condition, place cells maintained their representation until a threshold morph value ( S ≈ 0.25–0.50) and then coherently switched to a different representation ... This difference between conditions was also apparent in the normalized place cell population similarity matrices ( P < 0.0011, two-sided permutation test using animal identities (IDs), n = 12 mice)

statistics.about: z-scored place cell similarity matrices, rare minus frequent (Fig. 2h)
statistics.test: two-sided permutation test using animal identities

statistics.about: raw place cell similarity matrices, rare minus frequent (Fig. 2g)
statistics.test: two-sided permutation test of mice across conditions

outcomes.notes: The raw rare minus frequent difference has three entries outside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the 923 permutations under both speed readings (0 with 0.25 +0.037, 0.5 with 1 +0.031, 0.75 with 1 +0.034). No entry of the per-cell z-scored difference lies outside the range of all permutations, so that half of the criterion fails, and the criterion names no partial outcome; the outcome is not reproduced (partially reproduced before the first verification round). Its largest entries (0 with 0.25 +0.424, 0.25 with 0.75 -0.358) lie outside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles. Two variants of the 2020 code meet both halves: R6 counted as frequent (three z-scored entries outside the range), and unsmoothed maps (M5 variant, added after the first round; z-scored 0.25 with 0.5 -0.509 and 0.25 with 0.75 -0.508 outside the range, raw 0 with 0.25 +0.055 and +0.056 outside the percentiles, both speed readings). The criterion's smoothing decides. The rare morph mean similarity to S-tilde 0 is 0.939 at 0.25 and 0.854 at 0.5, the frequent 0.902 and 0.870, the threshold pattern of the statement.

outcomes.statement: Non-negative matrix factorization of single-cell trial-by-trial similarity matrices confirms discrete remapping in rare morph sessions and gradual remapping in frequent morph sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 6
outcomes.quote: These findings were also confirmed using a second unsupervised approach ... non-negative matrix factorization
outcomes.notes: The step share of the NMF factors is 0.763 for rare and 1.072 for frequent morph mice (difference -0.309, inside the permutation percentiles -0.627 to 0.627, and of the opposite sign). F5 raises the frequent mean (3.4, from one session at about 12.26); the other mice lie between 0.463 and 1.181. Two sessions have no factor whose largest block is an extreme. Seven sessions have a share above 1, as the share has no upper bound when a row is not monotone. Clipped at 1, rare 0.682 and frequent 0.657 (difference 0.025, percentiles -0.157 to 0.157); with per-mouse medians, difference 0.056 (percentiles -0.267 to 0.267). Neither is significant, so the outcome does not rest on the unbounded sessions.
deviations: NMF with nndsvda initialisation and an iteration limit of 2,000 (standard choices); one fit reached the limit.
The step share is the claims file's reading; the paper judges the factors by eye.

outcomes.statement: In a nonlinear embedding (UMAP) of the morph-by-position activity of task-modulated cells, cells from rare morph and frequent morph mice can be told apart.
outcomes.source: Results, Prior experience of stimulus frequency determines CA1 place cell remapping, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 5c
outcomes.quote: Rare and frequent morph cells were also separable using this approach.
outcomes.notes: The distance test keeps 18,742 cells (paper 18,230) and DBSCAN leaves 292 between two manifolds (paper 150). Rare against frequent classification beats all shuffles in 16 of 20 clusters against 100 shuffles and in 13 of 20 against 1,000, so both readings of "separable" hold for both shuffle counts. Accuracies 0.538 to 0.714; rare cells are 69% to 89% of a cluster. The UMAP layout, and so these counts, differ between runs although every seed is fixed (the kept cells do not); the run after the first verification round gave 17 and 16 of 20, the copy the second verifier read 16 of 20 against 100 shuffles, and both readings held in each run seen. The criterion's cross-validation splits cells, not mice. Holding out each mouse's cells in turn (added after the first verification round) gives a balanced accuracy of 0.372 to 0.688 (median 0.546), above 0.5 in 14 of 20 clusters and above the 95th percentile of 100 mouse relabelings in 5 of 20, so the separation within a cluster may in part reflect mouse identity. This check does not decide the outcome.
deviations: A cell is kept when its distance exceeds the 99.9th percentile of its 1,000 shuffles (a standard reading of "exceeded 99.9% of permutations"); the ten S bins are equal over -0.1 to 1.1 as the criterion says.
Logistic regression is fitted exactly (Newton's method) for all permutations at once, with sklearn's objective, splits and class weights; it matches sklearn's fit on test data.
The 2020 code's min_dist of 0.01 is shown for the first embedding and its manifold split only.

outcomes.statement: Well-trained mice ran steadily down the first half of the track and began licking as they approached the reward.
outcomes.source: Methods, Morphed environments, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 1c-g
outcomes.quote: Once the animals were well trained, they often ran consistently down the first half of the track and began licking as they approached the reward
outcomes.notes: For each 50 cm reward-location bin the across-mouse mean lick rate rises over the 50 cm before the reward (slopes 0.032 to 0.067 licks/s per cm) and peaks 5 cm into the bin (255, 305 and 355 cm with low-speed frames left out), and all 12 mice lick less over 0 to 225 cm than over 250 to 400 cm, under both speed readings. Running is not judged.
deviations: The rise is read as a positive slope over the 50 cm before the bin with the last bin above the first; within 50 cm as a peak from 50 cm before to 50 cm after the reward bin.
Licks are the file's per-frame lick series, which its description says not to use for comparisons between groups; only shapes within mice are used.

outcomes.statement: Single-session population trial-by-trial similarity matrices show two blocks in the rare morph condition and a gradual transition between the extremes in the frequent morph condition.
outcomes.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 3a,b; Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8
outcomes.quote: For the rare morph condition, a strong block diagonal structure in the trial-by-trial similarity matrices suggested clustering of morph values into two representations
outcomes.notes: The step share is 0.605 for rare (0.485 to 0.792) and 0.563 for frequent morph mice (0.434 to 0.749); the difference, 0.042, is inside the permutation percentiles (-0.116 to 0.116). The rare morph rows fall mostly between S-tilde 0.25 and 0.5, but the measure does not separate the groups. The dependency fig3f-zscored-difference-at-025 is reproduced. No mouse row has a step share above 1, so clipping the share at 1 changes nothing (difference 0.042).

outcomes.statement: In six named rare morph sessions, trials near S-tilde = 0.25 randomly take one extreme representation or the other, seen as checkerboard bands in the sorted similarity matrices.
outcomes.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraph 1; Extended Data Fig. 7
outcomes.quote: checker-board dark bands were observed in the similarity matrices near S ~ = 0.25 , as if the matrix was missorted for R1 session 8, R2 session 13, R3 session 9, R4 session 11, R5 session 8 and R6 session 10
outcomes.notes: Five of the six named sessions have S-tilde 0.25 trials with SF on both sides of 0.5 (R1 8, R2 13, R3 9, R4 11, R6 10); in R5 session 8 all 16 lie below 0.5 (0.424 to 0.465). The criterion asks all six and names no partial outcome, so the outcome is not reproduced (partially reproduced before the first verification round). Session numbers are the file names' days, which equal the JSON annotation's day. Against the deposit (vr-deposit-link), R5's file of day 8 is also the 8th task-track date of R5, so it is R5's session 8 under either numbering; for R1 to R4 and R6 the date ordinal is one or two higher than the file day. 18 of the 20 other rare sessions also have trials on both sides.

outcomes.statement: After z-scoring within session, trial-by-trial population similarity differs significantly between rare and frequent morph mice for S-tilde = 0.25 trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Population similarity analyses reveal distinct remapping patterns visible at the level of single trials, paragraph 3; Figure 3c-f
outcomes.quote: As predicted, group differences in trial-by-trial similarity were significant for S ~ = 0.25 trials after z -scoring within session similarity ( P < 0.05 two-sided mouse permutation test, n = 12 mice)
outcomes.notes: In the S-tilde 0.25 row the entries with 0.5 (-0.409) and 1.0 (-0.367) lie outside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the 923 permutations. All three variants (normalised signal, unsmoothed, z-scored mouse means) also find significant entries in that row.

outcomes.statement: Position-wise SF shows stable clustered representations along the whole track in rare morph mice and a spectrum in frequent morph mice; remapping happens soon after the trial starts and stays as the mouse runs.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 representations show stable discrimination of morph values along the length of the track, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 4b-e
outcomes.quote: Plotting SF as a function of the position of the animal along the VR track revealed a clustering of stable representations across the entire length of the track for the rare morph condition ... Together, these results indicate that remapping rapidly occurred after the start of a new trial and remained stable as the animal traversed the virtual track.
outcomes.notes: In both conditions the S-tilde 0 and 1 curves differ by more than their summed s.e.m. in all 44 bins after the first; in rare morph mice the 0.75 and 1.0 curves overlap in all 45 bins and the 0.25 curve is nearer the 0 curve in all 45; in frequent morph mice the 0.25 curve lies between the 0 and 0.5 curves in all 45.

outcomes.statement: Delta D_KL of each session's Q estimate took the expected sign (negative for rare, positive for frequent) in 41 of 45 sessions and in every session of 9 of 12 mice; across mice, rare -0.88 +- 0.23 and frequent 0.50 +- 0.11 (mean +- s.e.m.), a significant difference.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 2; Figure 6a
outcomes.quote: This Δ D KL measure took the expected sign (rare sessions Δ D KL < 0 and frequent sessions Δ D KL > 0) in 41 out of 45 sessions, and it took the expected sign in every session from 9 out of 12 mice (across animal mean±s.e.m.: rare Δ D KL = −0.88 ± 0.23, frequent Δ D KL = 0.50±0.11; P <0.0011, two-sided animal permutation test, n = 12 mice)
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. The priors now come from every trial before session 8 in the figshare deposit (data with inputs), not the dandiset's imaged trials; the rare prior holds 0.183 of its mass between 0.15 and 0.85 units, against 0.256 before. With the Methods likelihood the sign is as expected in 43 of 47 sessions (within 41 +- 4.1), the rare mean is -0.660 +- 0.104 (within -0.88 +- 0.23), the frequent mean 0.158 +- 0.052 (outside 0.50 +- 0.11, sign as expected), and 8 mice have the expected sign in every session (outside 9 +- 0.9). The difference, -0.817, lies outside the range of all 923 permutations (-0.727 to 0.817). With the earlier priors the values were 37 sessions, 7 mice, rare -0.354 and frequent 0.007, the same outcome. With the code's likelihood widths, variants, 44 and 40 sessions, 10 mice, rare -0.848 and -0.866, frequent 0.701 and 0.778.

outcomes.statement: Q estimates pooled over all sessions and mice approximate the posterior of the matching condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.44, frequent 0.42).
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 3; Figure 6b,c, left panels
outcomes.quote: Combining data from all sessions and all mice gave a robust approximation (Δ D KL ) of the posterior for both the rare morph and frequent morph conditions (rare Δ D KL = −0.44, frequent Δ D KL = 0.42
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors the pooled Q estimates give rare -0.464 and frequent 0.125 (reading a) and -0.469 and 0.118 (reading b), against -0.44 +- 0.044 and 0.42 +- 0.042. The rare value is within tolerance under both readings and the frequent value has the expected sign but is outside, so only the signs hold, the criterion's partial outcome. With the earlier priors from the dandiset's imaged trials the values were -0.266 and -0.000, and the outcome was not reproduced. With the code's likelihood widths, variants, frequent 0.590 to 0.646 and rare -0.259 to -0.360.

outcomes.statement: Priors reconstructed from each mouse's neural data alone are closer to the ideal prior of the mouse's own condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.46 +- 0.12, frequent 0.46 +- 0.07, mean +- s.e.m. across mice), a significant group difference.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 4; Figure 6b-d
outcomes.quote: A similar Δ D KL metric showed that the reconstructed priors are closer to the ideal prior from the correct condition than the ideal prior from the incorrect condition ( Fig. 6d ) (across animal mean±s.e.m.: rare Δ D KL = −0.46 ± 0.12, frequent Δ D KL = 0.46±0.07; P <0.0011, animal permutation test, n = 12 mice)
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors the difference of across-mouse means, -0.902, still lies outside the range of all permutations and all six frequent morph mice are positive (1.125 +- 0.076, outside 0.46 +- 0.07), but the rare morph mean is positive, 0.223 +- 0.122 (expected -0.46 +- 0.12), with only R3 (-0.033) and R6 (-0.166) negative. The sign of the rare mean fails, so the partial outcome (test and signs) is not met. With the earlier priors the rare mean was -0.020 and the frequent 0.633 and the outcome was partially reproduced; the rare prior from every trial has less intermediate mass, and the rare mice's reconstructions sit nearer the frequent prior. The code's likelihood widths, variants, give rare 0.480 and 0.517. After the first verification round an ideal-observer check was added. An observer whose estimates are drawn from the rare posterior, on each mouse's own trials, gives a reconstructed-prior Delta D_KL of +0.547 on average (0.380 to 0.741) under the criterion's formula, while its Q estimate gives -0.303; the frequent observer gives +1.003. So the formula cannot give the rare sign on this design. The paper's code computes R with Z taken at the grid point f (SFReg at dca5a57, which printed -0.476 +- 0.132 and 0.453 +- 0.074, and the 2026 code). With that computation, a variant, the ideal observers give +0.047 (rare) and +0.502 (frequent), and the data give rare -0.288 +- 0.127 (4 of 6 negative) and frequent 0.638 +- 0.078, the difference outside every permutation; with the 2020 code's likelihood width (0.3 units) and last-mouse prior as well, rare -0.421 +- 0.123 and frequent 0.500 +- 0.077, both within tolerance. The criterion fixes the Methods formula, so the outcome stands; a question asks a reader whether the claim should follow the code.

outcomes.statement: The average MAP estimate of f_h for S-tilde = 0 trials is 11.08 under the rare and 10.64 under the frequent posterior, and for S-tilde = 1 trials 38.13 and 37.30.
outcomes.source: Methods, Estimating posterior distributions from population activity (Q estimates)
outcomes.quote: average rare morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 0 trials: f h = 11.08; average frequent morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 0 trials: f h = 10.64; average rare morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 1 trials: f h = 38.13; average frequent morph MAP estimate for S ~ = 1 trials: f h = 37.30
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors, under reading (a) the means are 10.62, 10.69, 38.19 and 37.62 f_h, all within 10% of the paper's; reading (b) and the code's likelihood widths also give all four within 10%. The earlier priors gave 10.67, 10.72, 38.09 and 37.62, the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: The rare versus frequent remapping patterns were stable over sessions and emerged early in training (session 3) in most animals.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 9a-i
outcomes.quote: Of note, these remapping patterns observed in rare morph versus frequent morph conditions were stable over sessions and emerged early in training in most animals
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. Reading (a) uses the deposit's group posteriors, and reading (b) builds posteriors from every deposit trial before each mouse's session 3 (4 to 7 sessions, 320 to 517 trials per mouse, none intermediate for the rare morph mice), where the earlier run had only the dandiset's session 1 trials of 9 mice. Session 3 Delta D_KL has the expected sign in 8 of 11 mice under both readings (F2, R1 and R5 have the other sign under both). In sessions 8 to N every mouse has one sign in most of its sessions (67% to 100%). Same outcome as before.

outcomes.statement: For rare morph sessions, Q estimates are fit worse by the frequent, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal prior posteriors and by a uniform posterior than by the rare morph posterior.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 9j,k
outcomes.quote: Furthermore, a comparison of Q estimates to a number of other null model posteriors yielded poor fits to the data
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors, all five nulls fit the 26 rare morph sessions worse than the rare posterior in every session (Wilcoxon p = 3e-08 each), as before. With the code's likelihood widths, added after the first verification round, all five tests hold as well (p at most 0.00022).
deviations: 26 sessions, where the paper's tests used 24.

outcomes.statement: For frequent morph sessions, Q estimates are fit worse by the rare, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal prior posteriors and by a uniform posterior than by the frequent morph posterior.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 9l legend
outcomes.quote: Wilcoxon signed rank tests compare D KL for the frequent morph condition to D KL for all other posteriors in ( j )
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors four of five tests hold, rare posterior (frequent closer in 17 of 21 sessions, p = 0.00051), Gaussian prior (p = 9.5e-07), multimodal prior (p = 1.3e-05) and uniform posterior (p = 1.9e-06). The uniform prior does not (frequent closer in 5 of 21 sessions, p = 0.12). The criterion asks all five and names no partial outcome, so the outcome is not reproduced (partially reproduced before the first verification round). With the code's likelihood widths, added after that round, the uniform prior fails again (p = 0.18 and 0.29, frequent closer in 6 and 7 of 21) and the other four hold. With the earlier priors three held and the rare posterior was not worse (p = 0.37).

outcomes.statement: Frequent morph mice trained to report whether S was above or below 0.5 by where they licked (FD1 to FD4) remapped like frequent morph mice without the task.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 10
outcomes.quote: The remapping patterns were similar to those observed in frequent morph mice that did not perform this task
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the deposit's priors both readings hold. (a) The Q estimate pooled over the decision mice has Delta D_KL 0.042 over every imaged session and 0.125 over sessions 8 to N, where the earlier priors gave -0.042 and -0.006, so the outcome rises from partially reproduced. (b) Each decision mouse's reconstructed prior is closer to the frequent prior (0.933 to 1.082 over every imaged session, 0.970 to 1.128 over sessions 8 to N). FD1's sessions 1 and 3 have no S-tilde 0 or 1 trials and give no SF. Reading (b) carries little evidence under the criterion's formula, which is positive even for an ideal rare observer (+0.547, fig6d-prior-reconstruction). With the code's computation of R, a variant, under which the ideal rare observer gives +0.047 and the frequent one +0.502, the decision mice give 0.433 to 0.578 over every imaged session and 0.460 to 0.627 over sessions 8 to N. The 2020 code's sessions (5 and later), a variant, give a pooled value of 0.005 and reconstructions of 0.727 to 1.082. A question asks a reader whether the reconstruction should follow the code (fig6d-prior-reconstruction).

outcomes.statement: Of the stimulus features, the horizontal component of wall frequency f_h best predicts the first principal component of the variance across VR scenes.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 2g legend; Results, Two-photon imaging of CA1 cells in morphed VR environments, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The horizontal component of wall frequency, f h , is the strongest predictor of the projection onto PC1.
outcomes.notes: The test uses screenshots of the Unity scenes over the range of morph settings, which are not in the dandiset, and the paper names no other deposit for them.

outcomes.statement: A Hebbian network with radial basis inputs and k-winners-take-all competition, trained on stimuli drawn from the rare or frequent morph prior, gives Q estimates that match the matching posterior.
outcomes.source: Results, Simple associative-learning mechanisms can approximate probabilistic inference in neural populations, paragraph 1; Figure 7b-f
outcomes.quote: model-derived SF values and Q estimates were good matches to the appropriate posterior distributions
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. The criterion now gives the code's scale (inputs exp(-(mu - x)^2 / 0.15^2) in units, centres -0.1 to 1.1 units), stimulus, output and weight noise in training and testing, the losers' noise, and test stimuli at the f_h of S from -0.3 to 1.3; the priors come from the deposit (data elsewhere). The network now learns, the weights ending with a mean of 2.25 (rare-trained) and 2.77 (frequent-trained) and reaching the cap of 5, where under the earlier reading they decayed to 0.000004 or followed the noise. The median Delta D_KL of the 50 rare-trained models is -0.564 (all 50 below 0) and of the 50 frequent-trained models 0.093 (40 of 50 above 0), so the criterion holds; the code's likelihood widths, variants, and the earlier priors from the dandiset's trials give the same signs. The criterion says the test stimuli lie between 5.5 and 38.5 f_h; computed as it prescribes, they span 0.04 to 38.45 f_h, as f_h falls again for S below -0.1. A question asks a reader about the criterion's statement on the range of the test stimuli.
deviations: The losers' noise follows the Methods (all N - K losers), not the code's indexing slip, as the criterion says.
outcomes.where: figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31974756.v1 (Unprocessed VR data; the model needs only the priors of M7)

outcomes.statement: Priors reconstructed from the model's Q estimates are closer to the prior of the matching condition, though less closely matched than for the neural data.
outcomes.source: Results, Simple associative-learning mechanisms can approximate probabilistic inference in neural populations, paragraph 1; Figure 7g
outcomes.quote: These unsupervised reconstructions were quantitatively more similar to the prior of the matching condition, but the match between the reconstruction and the true priors was not as compelling as the match seen in the neural data.
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. With the models of fig7-model-reproduces-remapping as now specified and the deposit's priors, the averaged reconstructed prior has Delta D_KL -0.098 bits for the rare-trained and 0.626 bits for the frequent-trained models (-0.068 and 0.434 nats), both of the expected sign and smaller in magnitude than the neural across-mouse means of fig6d-prior-reconstruction (0.223 and 1.125), so the criterion's test passes as written. But the rare neural mean has the wrong sign, so the neural reconstructions of the rare morph mice do not match the rare prior and "less closely matched than for the neural data" is not shown for the rare condition. With the code's computation of R, a variant, the rare-trained models give -0.349 against a neural rare mean of -0.288 (a larger magnitude) and the frequent-trained 0.378 against 0.638. The signs hold under both computations and the comparison holds for the frequent condition only, so the outcome was given as partially reproduced after the first verification round. The criterion names no partial outcome and its test passes as written, so, as for session-and-trial-counts, fig2eh, edf7 and edf9l, the outcome is reproduced, proposed after the second round and agreed in the third. The rare half of the comparison carries little evidence, since the rare neural yardstick has the wrong sign and an ideal rare observer gets +0.547 under the Methods formula (nb2 cell 35). The earlier priors give -0.188 and 0.264. A question asks a reader whether the reconstruction should follow the code (fig6d-prior-reconstruction).

outcomes.statement: A simulated population that stochastically encodes samples from the rare or frequent morph posterior reproduces the recorded remapping patterns.
outcomes.source: Results, CA1 population activity approximates optimal estimation of the stimulus, paragraph 6; Extended Data Fig. 3
outcomes.quote: Simulating neural populations that were designed to stochastically encode the posterior distributions also reproduced the remapping patterns described above
outcomes.notes: What the answer changed. The neuron centres are evenly spaced over the M6 grid, as the earlier run had them; each simulation's trial matrix is now z-scored over its off-diagonal entries before averaging (the earlier run z-scored each session's block matrix), and the posteriors use the deposit's priors. The recorded S-tilde 0.25 row has significant entries at 0.5 (-0.409) and 1.0 (-0.367). The simulated difference over 1,000 simulations has the same sign at 0.5 under both readings (-0.410 and -0.444); at 1.0 it is -0.036 under reading (a) and +0.030 under reading (b), so the criterion, which asks both readings, is not met. The earlier z-scoring, a variant here, gives -0.006 and -0.004 at 1.0 with the deposit's posteriors; the earlier run had +0.009 under both readings.

outcomes.statement: With reasonable assumed priors, the probabilistic inference framework reproduces the discrete and gradual remapping reported in earlier morphed-environment studies (Wills 2005, Colgin 2010 double and single location, Leutgeb 2005).
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figs. 1 to 4
outcomes.quote: making reasonable assumptions, we reproduced each of the conflicting findings from previous studies using our probabilistic inference framework
outcomes.notes: A simulation with priors the authors propose for other laboratories' experiments; it uses no data of this paper, so the dandiset cannot test it.

findings.statement: Each file holds only the imaged trials of its session, and sessions without imaging (2, 4 and 6) are absent. The paper's priors and its training statistics use every trial a mouse ran before session 8, so these cannot be rebuilt from the dandiset alone. The authors' figshare deposit (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31974756.v1) holds every VR session, and this attempt uses it, but neither the dandiset nor the paper's data statement names it.

The figshare VR deposit names mice by alias (for example 4139265.3) and the dandiset by R1 to FD4; no NWB file records the alias, so the link rests on the mapping in the authors' 2026 code (mouse_metadata.py). The trial sequences confirm that mapping for all 89 files of the rare and frequent morph mice.

The deposit's session database flags 26 VR sessions of the rare and frequent morph mice as imaged that have no file in the dandiset (12 of them R6's, on seven dates, five before its session 8 and two after it), without a note on why they were left out.
Mouse R6 has no session before 8 in the dandiset, R4 and R5 lack session 1, and FD3 has no session after 7, so the decision-mouse trial counts cannot match the paper's.

The dandiset holds imaging sessions 5 and 7 for most mice (and session 6 for R4), which the paper does not list among its imaging sessions (1, 3 and 8 to N), and 26 rare morph sessions 8 to N where the paper counts 24. F6 session 5 has 4,103 cells, above the paper's stated range.
The session_start_time of every file is the date of conversion in April 2026, not the date of the recording, so the calendar days between sessions cannot be read from the files.
The decision mouse FD1's sessions 1 and 3 hold continuous morph values in place of the five S-tilde values, and nothing in the files or the dandiset says so.

The JSON annotation of each file stores place cells from the authors' 2026 code. They agree with this attempt's no-speed-exclusion reading for about 96% of cell and S-tilde pairs and give 61.5% (rare) and 48.6% (frequent) of cells as place cells, against the paper's 43% and 30%.

The published versions of 2021 hold 85 files for 10 of the 16 mice (F4, F6 and the decision mice are missing); the versions of April 2026 hold all 16. Version 0.260415.1712 replaced R5's files and removed its sessions 1, 5 and 7 relative to 0.260409.0433, without release notes.

The file names' session days are not the ordinal of the recording date among each mouse's task-track dates in the authors' VR deposit for R1 to R4, R6 and F4 (one date higher, two for R6): the deposit holds eight task-track dates before session 8 for these mice (nine for R6), one more than sessions 1 to 7 (two more for R6). Neither the dandiset nor the deposit says how sessions were numbered.

verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The handover of the author-answers run (commit 2c4f3f2826): the executed notebooks with the conclusions and summary removed, the helper module and the claims file; the verifier also read the paper under paper/ and the archive's asset list.

disagreements.reason: Rare 26 sessions and 2,800 trials, frequent 21 and 1,986: all within tolerance. Decision-mouse trials are 3,217 under reading (a) and 2,022 under (b), against 2,460 +- 246 (nb1 cell 11).

No z-scored entry lies outside the range of the 923 permutations, under either speed reading. The raw matrix does pass at the 95% level. Only the 2020-code variant that counts R6 as frequent passes (nb1 cell 22).

R5 session 8: 0 of 16 S-tilde = 0.25 trials have SF above 0.5 (range 0.424 to 0.465). The other five named sessions pass (nb2 cell 15). The notebook assumes file "day" equals the paper's session number without showing it (problem 3).
The uniform-prior null gives p = 0.12 and a median of -0.018; the frequent posterior is closer in only 5 of 21 sessions (nb2 cell 31).

The signs are right (-0.098 and +0.626 bits). The magnitude test passes as written, but only because the neural rare mean it is compared with (+0.223) has the wrong sign. The "less closely matched than neural" half is therefore not shown for rare (nb2 cell 36).

paper_notes.statement: The Methods give the Hebbian model's input width as "σ 2 = 4.11" in f_h; the paper's code uses a width sigma of 0.15 units (4.11 f_h, so a denominator of 16.9 f_h^2) and a stimulus noise of 0.1 units, and read as a variance in f_h the model's weights decay to zero during training.

The prior reconstruction in the paper's code (SFReg.plot_sfreg at dca5a57; similarity_fraction.single_sess_reconstruction at 9230b0a) divides by sum_j L(f, x_j) / Z(f), taking the normalising constant Z at the grid point f, where the Methods formula sums L(fhat | f) / Z(fhat) over fhat. The code printed -0.476 +- 0.132 and 0.453 +- 0.074, the paper's values. On this task's trial design the Methods formula gives a positive Delta D_KL even for an ideal observer sampling the rare posterior (+0.547 here).

entries.name: plitt-2021
entries.title: Experience-dependent contextual codes in the hippocampus (Plitt and Giocomo 2021)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Plitt and Giocomo (2021) on dandiset 000054, which holds the two-photon imaging of CA1 and the aligned virtual reality behaviour of 16 mice running morphed linear tracks. Part 1 covers sessions, licking, place cells, their similarity matrices, NMF and UMAP; part 2 covers the link to the authors' VR deposit on figshare and the training trials, population similarity, the similarity fraction, Q estimates, prior reconstruction, the decision mice and the two models.
